tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

1	# Concept 1: AI Planning Collaboration
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	Learn to collaborate with AI during the architectural planning phase. You'll use AI to explore design alternatives, evaluate trade-offs, and create a solid foundation for implementation—all while maintaining ownership of engineering decisions.
6	
7	## Learning Objectives
8	
9	- Use structured XML prompts to guide AI through architectural exploration
10	- Evaluate multiple architectural alternatives with clear trade-off analysis
11	- Design modular systems with clear responsibilities and interfaces
12	- Make informed architectural decisions based on engineering principles
13	- Create implementation roadmaps that guide development
14	
15	## Exercise Structure
16	
17	This exercise has two parts:
18	
19	- **Part A (Guided Practice)**: Plan an expense tracker architecture to learn the methodology
20	- **Part B (Your Project)**: Apply the same techniques to plan your own application
21	
22	The goal is to master the planning process,not to become an expense tracker expert.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## Part A: Guided Practice - Expense Tracker Planning
27	
28	### Scenario
29	
30	You're building a CLI expense tracker that helps users analyze their spending from CSV transaction files. The application should support different types of reports (by category, by month, etc.) and be easily extensible for new report types.
31	
32	### Functional Requirements
33	
34	- Load expense transactions from CSV files
35	- Support multiple report modes: summary by category, monthly totals
36	- Display formatted reports in the terminal
37	- Calculate totals and provide accurate summaries
38	- Handle invalid data gracefully
39	
40	### Technical Requirements
41	
42	- Python 3.8+ with standard library only
43	- Modular architecture following SOLID principles
44	- Strategy pattern for different report types
45	- Clean separation: data loading, business logic, UI
46	- Comprehensive error handling
47	
48	---
49	
50	## Step 1: Architectural Exploration (15 minutes)
51	
52	Use AI to generate 2-3 architectural alternatives. Copy this prompt template and use it with your AI assistant:
53	
54	```xml
55	<role>Senior Python architect with expertise in SOLID principles and design patterns</role>
56	
57	<task>
58	Evaluate and compare 2-3 architectural approaches for a CLI expense tracker application
59	</task>
60	
61	<context>
62	<application_type>Command-line personal finance report generator</application_type>
63	<tech_stack>Python 3.8+, CSV file storage, terminal interface</tech_stack>
64	<user_workflow>Load transactions from CSV → Select report mode → View formatted report</user_workflow>
65	<data_structure>Transactions with date, description, category, amount (negative for expenses)</data_structure>
66	</context>
67	
68	<requirements>
69	<functional_requirements>
70	- Load and validate expense transactions from CSV files
71	- Support multiple report modes (summary by category, monthly totals, etc.)
72	- Display formatted reports in terminal with totals
73	- Handle invalid data and missing files gracefully
74	- Track and display summary statistics
75	</functional_requirements>
76	
77	<extensibility_requirements>
78	- Easy to add new report modes without modifying existing code
79	- Support for different data formats (JSON, etc.) in future
80	- Configurable report formatting and display options
81	- Plugin architecture for custom report types
82	</extensibility_requirements>
83	
84	<quality_attributes>
85	- High testability with minimal mocking required
86	- Clear separation of concerns (data, logic, UI)
87	- Minimal coupling between components
88	- Single responsibility for each module
89	</quality_attributes>
90	</requirements>
91	
92	<constraints>
93	<architecture_principles>Follow SOLID principles explicitly</architecture_principles>
94	<complexity_limits>Keep each module under 200 lines, single responsibility</complexity_limits>
95	<dependencies>Standard library only, no external frameworks</dependencies>
96	<error_handling>Comprehensive validation and clear error messages</error_handling>
97	</constraints>
98	
99	<deliverables>
100	- 2-3 distinct architectural approaches with trade-offs
101	- Specific design patterns to use and why (Strategy, Factory, etc.)
102	- Module responsibilities and interfaces
103	- Extension points for future report types
104	- Recommendation with justification
105	</deliverables>
106	```
107	
108	**What to do with AI's response:**
109	1. Read through each architectural alternative carefully
110	2. Note the trade-offs for each approach
111	3. Consider: Which approach makes testing easier? Which is more extensible? Which is simpler to implement?
112	4. Don't just accept AI's recommendation—evaluate it against your own judgment
113	
114	**Document your findings** in `architecture_plan.md`:
115	- List the alternatives AI suggested
116	- Note the key trade-offs
117	- State which you'd choose and why
118	
119	---
120	
121	## Step 2: Module Design (15 minutes)
122	
123	Once you've selected an architecture, use AI to design the specific modules and interfaces:
124	
125	```xml
126	<role>Senior Python developer expert in module design and interface definition</role>
127	
128	<task>
129	Design detailed module structure and interfaces for expense tracker using [YOUR CHOSEN ARCHITECTURE]
130	</task>
131	
132	<context>
133	<selected_architecture>
134	[Paste the architecture you selected from Step 1]
135	</selected_architecture>
136	<design_principles>SOLID principles, dependency injection, interface segregation</design_principles>
137	<integration_requirements>Modules must integrate smoothly with minimal coupling</integration_requirements>
138	</context>
139	
140	<requirements>
141	<module_specifications>
142	- Each module has single, clear responsibility
143	- Public interfaces with complete type hints
144	- Private implementation details hidden
145	- Minimal dependencies between modules
146	</module_specifications>
147	
148	<interface_design>
149	- Method signatures with type annotations
150	- Docstring specifications (purpose, params, returns, raises)
151	- Error handling strategy for each module
152	- Input validation boundaries
153	</interface_design>
154	
155	<core_modules>
156	1. TransactionLoader - CSV loading and validation
157	2. ReportMode (Protocol/ABC) - Interface for report strategies
158	3. ReportEngine - Orchestrates report generation
159	4. CLIInterface - Terminal UI and user interaction
160	</core_modules>
161	
162	<data_models>
163	- Transaction representation (date, description, category, amount)
164	- Report data structure
165	- Error types (FileNotFoundError, ValidationError, etc.)
166	</data_models>
167	</requirements>
168	
169	<constraints>
170	<implementation_guidelines>
171	- Interfaces are minimal and focused
172	- No circular dependencies
173	- Design for testability (dependency injection)
174	- Extension points clearly identified
175	</implementation_guidelines>
176	</constraints>
177	
178	<deliverables>
179	- Module responsibility descriptions
180	- Interface definitions with type hints (as Python Protocol or ABC)
181	- Data model specifications
182	- Dependency diagram showing relationships
183	</deliverables>
184	```
185	
186	**What to do with AI's response:**
187	1. Review each module's responsibility—is it focused and clear?
188	2. Check interfaces—are they minimal and testable?
189	3. Look for circular dependencies—none should exist
190	4. Verify extension points—can new report modes be added easily?
191	
192	**Create `interfaces.py`** with the interface definitions AI suggested (as Protocols or ABCs).
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Step 3: Project Structure (10 minutes)
197	
198	Generate the complete directory structure:
199	
200	```xml
201	<role>Senior Python developer expert in project organization</role>
202	
203	<task>
204	Create comprehensive project directory structure for CLI expense tracker
205	</task>
206	
207	<context>
208	<modules>
209	[List the modules from Step 2]
210	</modules>
211	<architecture>
212	[Brief description of chosen architecture]
213	</architecture>
214	</context>
215	
216	<requirements>
217	<source_organization>
218	- Logical grouping of related modules
219	- Clear entry point (main.py)
220	- Utility modules in dedicated folder
221	- Sample data for development/testing
222	</source_organization>
223	
224	<testing_structure>
225	- Test directory mirroring source structure
226	- Unit tests for each module
227	- Integration tests for workflows
228	- Test fixtures and mock data
229	</testing_structure>
230	
231	<development_support>
232	- README with setup and usage
233	- requirements.txt (even if empty for stdlib-only)
234	- Sample CSV files for testing
235	- Documentation folder structure
236	</development_support>
237	</requirements>
238	
239	<constraints>
240	- Follow Python packaging best practices
241	- Use standard directory names
242	- Clear naming conventions
243	- Support development and distribution
244	</constraints>
245	
246	<deliverables>
247	- Complete directory tree with explanations
248	- File naming conventions
249	- Import path strategy
250	</deliverables>
251	```
252	
253	**Create `project_structure.txt`** showing your planned directory layout.
254	
255	---
256	
257	## Deliverables for Part A
258	
259	In the `starter/` folder, create these files:
260	
261	### 1. `architecture_plan.md`
262	Document your architectural decisions:
263	- **Alternatives Considered**: What options did AI suggest?
264	- **Trade-off Analysis**: Pros/cons of each approach
265	- **Selected Architecture**: Your choice with justification
266	- **Module Design**: Responsibilities and interfaces
267	- **Extension Strategy**: How to add new features
268	- **Implementation Roadmap**: Order of development
269	
270	### 2. `interfaces.py`
271	Python code with interface definitions:
272	```python
273	"""
274	Core interfaces for expense tracker application.
275	"""
276	from typing import Protocol, List, Dict
277	from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
278	
279	class ReportMode(Protocol):
280	    """Protocol defining interface for report generation strategies."""
281	
282	    def process_transactions(self, transactions: List[Dict]) -> Dict:
283	        """Process transactions and return report data."""
284	        ...
285	
286	class TransactionLoader(Protocol):
287	    """Protocol for loading and validating transactions."""
288	
289	    def load(self, filepath: str) -> List[Dict]:
290	        """Load transactions from file with validation."""
291	        ...
292	
293	# Add other interfaces based on your architecture
294	```
295	
296	### 3. `project_structure.txt`
297	```
298	expense-tracker/
299	├── main.py                    # CLI entry point
300	├── utils/
301	│   ├── __init__.py
302	│   ├── transaction_loader.py  # CSV loading
303	│   ├── report_engine.py       # Core orchestration
304	│   ├── report_modes.py        # Strategy implementations
305	│   └── cli_interface.py       # Terminal UI
306	├── tests/
307	│   ├── __init__.py
308	│   ├── test_transaction_loader.py
309	│   ├── test_report_engine.py
310	│   ├── test_report_modes.py
311	│   └── test_cli_interface.py
312	├── data/
313	│   └── sample_expenses.csv    # Sample data
314	├── README.md
315	└── requirements.txt
316	```
317	
318	---
319	
320	## Part B: Apply to Your Project
321	
322	Now apply the same planning methodology to your own application idea.
323	
324	### Step 1: Define Your Project
325	
326	Choose what you want to build:
327	- **Personal productivity**: Task manager, habit tracker, note organizer
328	- **Educational tools**: Vocabulary builder, study scheduler, math practice
329	- **Utilities**: File organizer, log analyzer, data converter
330	- **Simple games**: Text adventure, quiz game, number puzzle
331	- **Data tools**: CSV processor, report generator, configuration manager
332	
333	### Step 2: Adapt the Prompts
334	
335	Take the XML prompt templates from Part A and adapt them for your domain:
336	- Change `<application_type>` to your app type
337	- Modify `<functional_requirements>` for your features
338	- Update `<data_structure>` for your data models
339	- Adjust `<design_patterns>` for your specific needs
340	
341	### Step 3: Document Your Plan
342	
343	Create `my_project_plan.md` with:
344	1. **Project Vision**: What you're building and why
345	2. **Requirements Analysis**: Functional and technical requirements
346	3. **Architectural Alternatives**: Options explored with trade-offs
347	4. **Selected Architecture**: Your choice with justification
348	5. **Module Design**: Interfaces and responsibilities
349	6. **Implementation Roadmap**: Development order and phases
350	
351	---
352	
353	## Validation
354	
355	Run the provided test to validate your planning:
356	
357	```bash
358	cd starter/
359	pytest test_planning_process.py -v
360	```
361	
362	This test checks:
363	- ✅ `architecture_plan.md` exists and has required sections
364	- ✅ `interfaces.py` contains properly defined interfaces
365	- ✅ `project_structure.txt` shows logical organization
366	- ✅ Interfaces follow Protocol or ABC patterns
367	- ✅ No obvious circular dependencies in design
368	
369	---
370	
371	## Tips for Success
372	
373	1. **Don't accept first suggestion**: Use `<deliverables>` to request alternatives
374	2. **Question AI's recommendations**: Apply your engineering judgment
375	3. **Focus on extensibility**: Make adding features easy
376	4. **Design for testability**: Dependency injection, clear interfaces
377	5. **Keep it simple**: Resist over-engineering temptation
378	6. **Document rationale**: Capture why you made decisions
379	
380	## Common Pitfalls to Avoid
381	
382	❌ **Accepting AI's first suggestion without evaluation**
383	✅ Request alternatives and analyze trade-offs
384	
385	❌ **Over-engineering the architecture**
386	✅ Start simple, add complexity only when justified
387	
388	❌ **Skipping interface definitions**
389	✅ Clear interfaces enable independent module development
390	
391	❌ **Ignoring testability in design**
392	✅ Design for dependency injection and minimal mocking
393	
394	❌ **Circular dependencies between modules**
395	✅ Use dependency injection and interface segregation
396	
397	---
398	
399	## Time Estimate

401	- **Part A (Guided)**: 40 minutes

# Concept 1: AI Planning Collaboration

## Overview

Learn to collaborate with AI during the architectural planning phase. You'll use AI to explore design alternatives, evaluate trade-offs, and create a solid foundation for implementation—all while maintaining ownership of engineering decisions.

## Learning Objectives

- Use structured XML prompts to guide AI through architectural exploration
- Evaluate multiple architectural alternatives with clear trade-off analysis
- Design modular systems with clear responsibilities and interfaces
- Make informed architectural decisions based on engineering principles
- Create implementation roadmaps that guide development

## Exercise Structure

This exercise has two parts:

- **Part A (Guided Practice)**: Plan an expense tracker architecture to learn the methodology
- **Part B (Your Project)**: Apply the same techniques to plan your own application

The goal is to master the planning process,not to become an expense tracker expert.

---

## Part A: Guided Practice - Expense Tracker Planning

### Scenario

You're building a CLI expense tracker that helps users analyze their spending from CSV transaction files. The application should support different types of reports (by category, by month, etc.) and be easily extensible for new report types.

### Functional Requirements

- Load expense transactions from CSV files
- Support multiple report modes: summary by category, monthly totals
- Display formatted reports in the terminal
- Calculate totals and provide accurate summaries
- Handle invalid data gracefully

### Technical Requirements

- Python 3.8+ with standard library only
- Modular architecture following SOLID principles
- Strategy pattern for different report types
- Clean separation: data loading, business logic, UI
- Comprehensive error handling

---

## Step 1: Architectural Exploration (15 minutes)

Use AI to generate 2-3 architectural alternatives. Copy this prompt template and use it with your AI assistant:

```xml
<role>Senior Python architect with expertise in SOLID principles and design patterns</role>

<task>
Evaluate and compare 2-3 architectural approaches for a CLI expense tracker application
</task>

<context>
<application_type>Command-line personal finance report generator</application_type>
<tech_stack>Python 3.8+, CSV file storage, terminal interface</tech_stack>
<user_workflow>Load transactions from CSV → Select report mode → View formatted report</user_workflow>
<data_structure>Transactions with date, description, category, amount (negative for expenses)</data_structure>
</context>

<requirements>
<functional_requirements>
- Load and validate expense transactions from CSV files
- Support multiple report modes (summary by category, monthly totals, etc.)
- Display formatted reports in terminal with totals
- Handle invalid data and missing files gracefully
- Track and display summary statistics
</functional_requirements>

<extensibility_requirements>
- Easy to add new report modes without modifying existing code
- Support for different data formats (JSON, etc.) in future
- Configurable report formatting and display options
- Plugin architecture for custom report types
</extensibility_requirements>

<quality_attributes>
- High testability with minimal mocking required
- Clear separation of concerns (data, logic, UI)
- Minimal coupling between components
- Single responsibility for each module
</quality_attributes>
</requirements>

<constraints>
<architecture_principles>Follow SOLID principles explicitly</architecture_principles>
<complexity_limits>Keep each module under 200 lines, single responsibility</complexity_limits>
<dependencies>Standard library only, no external frameworks</dependencies>
<error_handling>Comprehensive validation and clear error messages</error_handling>
</constraints>

<deliverables>
- 2-3 distinct architectural approaches with trade-offs
- Specific design patterns to use and why (Strategy, Factory, etc.)
- Module responsibilities and interfaces
- Extension points for future report types
- Recommendation with justification
</deliverables>
```

**What to do with AI's response:**
1. Read through each architectural alternative carefully
2. Note the trade-offs for each approach
3. Consider: Which approach makes testing easier? Which is more extensible? Which is simpler to implement?
4. Don't just accept AI's recommendation—evaluate it against your own judgment

**Document your findings** in `architecture_plan.md`:
- List the alternatives AI suggested
- Note the key trade-offs
- State which you'd choose and why

---

## Step 2: Module Design (15 minutes)

Once you've selected an architecture, use AI to design the specific modules and interfaces:

```xml
<role>Senior Python developer expert in module design and interface definition</role>

<task>
Design detailed module structure and interfaces for expense tracker using [YOUR CHOSEN ARCHITECTURE]
</task>

<context>
<selected_architecture>
[Paste the architecture you selected from Step 1]
</selected_architecture>
<design_principles>SOLID principles, dependency injection, interface segregation</design_principles>
<integration_requirements>Modules must integrate smoothly with minimal coupling</integration_requirements>
</context>

<requirements>
<module_specifications>
- Each module has single, clear responsibility
- Public interfaces with complete type hints
- Private implementation details hidden
- Minimal dependencies between modules
</module_specifications>

<interface_design>
- Method signatures with type annotations
- Docstring specifications (purpose, params, returns, raises)
- Error handling strategy for each module
- Input validation boundaries
</interface_design>

<core_modules>
1. TransactionLoader - CSV loading and validation
2. ReportMode (Protocol/ABC) - Interface for report strategies
3. ReportEngine - Orchestrates report generation
4. CLIInterface - Terminal UI and user interaction
</core_modules>

<data_models>
- Transaction representation (date, description, category, amount)
- Report data structure
- Error types (FileNotFoundError, ValidationError, etc.)
</data_models>
</requirements>

<constraints>
<implementation_guidelines>
- Interfaces are minimal and focused
- No circular dependencies
- Design for testability (dependency injection)
- Extension points clearly identified
</implementation_guidelines>
</constraints>

<deliverables>
- Module responsibility descriptions
- Interface definitions with type hints (as Python Protocol or ABC)
- Data model specifications
- Dependency diagram showing relationships
</deliverables>
```

**What to do with AI's response:**
1. Review each module's responsibility—is it focused and clear?
2. Check interfaces—are they minimal and testable?
3. Look for circular dependencies—none should exist
4. Verify extension points—can new report modes be added easily?

**Create `interfaces.py`** with the interface definitions AI suggested (as Protocols or ABCs).

---

## Step 3: Project Structure (10 minutes)

Generate the complete directory structure:

```xml
<role>Senior Python developer expert in project organization</role>

<task>
Create comprehensive project directory structure for CLI expense tracker
</task>

<context>
<modules>
[List the modules from Step 2]
</modules>
<architecture>
[Brief description of chosen architecture]
</architecture>
</context>

<requirements>
<source_organization>
- Logical grouping of related modules
- Clear entry point (main.py)
- Utility modules in dedicated folder
- Sample data for development/testing
</source_organization>

<testing_structure>
- Test directory mirroring source structure
- Unit tests for each module
- Integration tests for workflows
- Test fixtures and mock data
</testing_structure>

<development_support>
- README with setup and usage
- requirements.txt (even if empty for stdlib-only)
- Sample CSV files for testing
- Documentation folder structure
</development_support>
</requirements>

<constraints>
- Follow Python packaging best practices
- Use standard directory names
- Clear naming conventions
- Support development and distribution
</constraints>

<deliverables>
- Complete directory tree with explanations
- File naming conventions
- Import path strategy
</deliverables>
```

**Create `project_structure.txt`** showing your planned directory layout.

---

## Deliverables for Part A

In the `starter/` folder, create these files:

### 1. `architecture_plan.md`
Document your architectural decisions:
- **Alternatives Considered**: What options did AI suggest?
- **Trade-off Analysis**: Pros/cons of each approach
- **Selected Architecture**: Your choice with justification
- **Module Design**: Responsibilities and interfaces
- **Extension Strategy**: How to add new features
- **Implementation Roadmap**: Order of development

### 2. `interfaces.py`
Python code with interface definitions:
```python
"""
Core interfaces for expense tracker application.
"""
from typing import Protocol, List, Dict
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class ReportMode(Protocol):
    """Protocol defining interface for report generation strategies."""

    def process_transactions(self, transactions: List[Dict]) -> Dict:
        """Process transactions and return report data."""
        ...

class TransactionLoader(Protocol):
    """Protocol for loading and validating transactions."""

    def load(self, filepath: str) -> List[Dict]:
        """Load transactions from file with validation."""
        ...

# Add other interfaces based on your architecture
```

### 3. `project_structure.txt`
```
expense-tracker/
├── main.py                    # CLI entry point
├── utils/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── transaction_loader.py  # CSV loading
│   ├── report_engine.py       # Core orchestration
│   ├── report_modes.py        # Strategy implementations
│   └── cli_interface.py       # Terminal UI
├── tests/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── test_transaction_loader.py
│   ├── test_report_engine.py
│   ├── test_report_modes.py
│   └── test_cli_interface.py
├── data/
│   └── sample_expenses.csv    # Sample data
├── README.md
└── requirements.txt
```

---

## Part B: Apply to Your Project

Now apply the same planning methodology to your own application idea.

### Step 1: Define Your Project

Choose what you want to build:
- **Personal productivity**: Task manager, habit tracker, note organizer
- **Educational tools**: Vocabulary builder, study scheduler, math practice
- **Utilities**: File organizer, log analyzer, data converter
- **Simple games**: Text adventure, quiz game, number puzzle
- **Data tools**: CSV processor, report generator, configuration manager

### Step 2: Adapt the Prompts

Take the XML prompt templates from Part A and adapt them for your domain:
- Change `<application_type>` to your app type
- Modify `<functional_requirements>` for your features
- Update `<data_structure>` for your data models
- Adjust `<design_patterns>` for your specific needs

### Step 3: Document Your Plan

Create `my_project_plan.md` with:
1. **Project Vision**: What you're building and why
2. **Requirements Analysis**: Functional and technical requirements
3. **Architectural Alternatives**: Options explored with trade-offs
4. **Selected Architecture**: Your choice with justification
5. **Module Design**: Interfaces and responsibilities
6. **Implementation Roadmap**: Development order and phases

---

## Validation

Run the provided test to validate your planning:

```bash
cd starter/
pytest test_planning_process.py -v
```

This test checks:
- ✅ `architecture_plan.md` exists and has required sections
- ✅ `interfaces.py` contains properly defined interfaces
- ✅ `project_structure.txt` shows logical organization
- ✅ Interfaces follow Protocol or ABC patterns
- ✅ No obvious circular dependencies in design

---

## Tips for Success

1. **Don't accept first suggestion**: Use `<deliverables>` to request alternatives
2. **Question AI's recommendations**: Apply your engineering judgment
3. **Focus on extensibility**: Make adding features easy
4. **Design for testability**: Dependency injection, clear interfaces
5. **Keep it simple**: Resist over-engineering temptation
6. **Document rationale**: Capture why you made decisions

## Common Pitfalls to Avoid

❌ **Accepting AI's first suggestion without evaluation**
✅ Request alternatives and analyze trade-offs

❌ **Over-engineering the architecture**
✅ Start simple, add complexity only when justified

❌ **Skipping interface definitions**
✅ Clear interfaces enable independent module development

❌ **Ignoring testability in design**
✅ Design for dependency injection and minimal mocking

❌ **Circular dependencies between modules**
✅ Use dependency injection and interface segregation

---

## Time Estimate

- **Part A (Guided)**: 40 minutes
- **Part B (Your Project)**: 30-40 minutes
- **Total**: ~70-80 minutes

## Next Steps

In Concept 2, you'll use AI to generate the actual code for the modules you've designed here. Having a clear plan makes code generation much more effective!

---

## Resources

- Review Lesson 3 for XML prompting techniques
- Reference SOLID principles when evaluating architectures
- Check solution folder for example complete planning documents

        try:

            pytest.fail(f"interfaces.py has syntax errors: {e}")

        """Should use Protocol or ABC for interface definitions."""
        has_protocol = False

        for node in ast.walk(interfaces_module):

                    has_abc = True

        assert has_protocol or has_abc, """
        interfaces.py should use Protocol or ABC for interface definitions.

        from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

        class TransactionLoader(ABC):

            def load(self, filepath: str) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
                pass

        """Interface classes should have docstrings."""
        classes = [node for node in ast.walk(interfaces_module) if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef)]

        for cls in classes:

            if not docstring:

"""Immutable domain value types shared by every layer of the expense tracker.

These types are the *currency* of the pipeline: a loader produces
``Transaction`` objects, a report mode consumes them and produces a ``Report``,
and a formatter consumes the ``Report``. Because every boundary speaks in these
types, each layer can be tested by constructing them directly -- no filesystem,
no stdout, no mocks.

All types are ``NamedTuple`` subclasses, which gives us for free:

* immutability (a report mode cannot corrupt the caller's data),
* structural equality (``assert result == expected`` in tests just works),
* a readable ``repr`` for test failure output,
* zero dependencies beyond the standard library.

Monetary amounts are ``decimal.Decimal``, never ``float``. Binary floating
point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so summing float amounts produces totals
like ``19.999999999999996``. ``Decimal`` is exact for base-10 fractions, which
is what money is.

In the shipped package this module lives at ``src/expense_tracker/models.py``.
It sits at the repository root here so the planning artifacts remain a
self-contained, importable set.
"""
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Sequence, Tuple


class Transaction(NamedTupleBase := __import__("typing").NamedTuple):
    """A single validated expense record loaded from a data source.

    A ``Transaction`` is only ever created by a :class:`TransactionLoader`
    implementation, and only after validation has succeeded. Downstream code
    may therefore assume every field is present and well-typed -- report modes
    should not re-check for ``None`` or attempt string parsing.

    Attributes:
        date: The calendar date the expense occurred, as a ``datetime.date``.
            Already parsed; never a string.
        amount: The expense amount as an exact ``Decimal``. Positive for
            spending. Never a ``float``.
        category: Non-empty category label, already stripped of surrounding
            whitespace (e.g. ``"Groceries"``).
        description: Free-text description. May be an empty string -- an
            absent description is not a validation failure -- but is never
            ``None``.
    """

    date: date
    amount: Decimal
    category: str
    description: str


class ReportRow(NamedTupleBase):
    """One aggregated line in a report.

    A row is the output of grouping, not a raw transaction. ``label`` is
    whatever the report mode grouped by -- a category name, a ``"2026-09"``
    month key, an ISO week -- and the formatter treats it as an opaque string.

    Attributes:
        label: The group key, rendered for display.
        amount: Sum of the amounts in this group, as an exact ``Decimal``.
        count: How many transactions were folded into this row. Defaults to 1
            so single-transaction rows need not pass it explicitly.
    """

    label: str
    amount: Decimal
    count: int = 1


class Report(NamedTupleBase):
    """The complete result of running one report mode over a transaction set.

    This is the only type a :class:`ReportMode` may return. Keeping the return
    shape fixed is what allows the formatting layer to stay generic: a new
    report mode never requires a new formatter.

    Attributes:
        title: Human-readable heading, supplied by the report mode
            (e.g. ``"Spending by Category"``).
        rows: The aggregated rows, in the order the mode chose. Ordering is
            part of each mode's own contract -- the formatter never re-sorts.
        total: Sum of ``row.amount`` across all rows. Stored rather than
            recomputed so a mode can define a total that is not a plain sum
            (an average, a net figure) without fighting the type.
    """

    title: str
    rows: Tuple[ReportRow, ...]
    total: Decimal

    @classmethod
    def empty(cls, title: str) -> "Report":
        """Build the canonical empty report.

        Report modes must return this (rather than ``None`` or raising) when
        given no transactions, or when no transaction matches their criteria.
        That is what makes every mode substitutable for every other -- see the
        Liskov note in ``interfaces.py``.

        Args:
            title: The heading the report would have carried had it had rows.

        Returns:
            A ``Report`` with no rows and a zero total.
        """
        return cls(title=title, rows=(), total=Decimal("0"))

    @property
    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Whether the report produced no rows.

        Formatters use this to print "No transactions matched." instead of an
        empty table with a lonely 0.00 total.
        """
        return len(self.rows) == 0

    @property
    def transaction_count(self) -> int:
        """Total number of transactions represented across all rows."""
        return sum(row.count for row in self.rows)


def sum_amounts(rows: Sequence[ReportRow]) -> Decimal:
    """Sum the amounts of a row sequence, returning an exact ``Decimal``.

    A convenience for report modes building a ``Report``: ``sum()`` on an empty
    sequence returns the integer ``0``, which would make ``Report.total``
    inconsistently typed. This always returns a ``Decimal``.

    Args:
        rows: The rows to total. May be empty.

    Returns:
        The exact sum, or ``Decimal("0")`` for an empty sequence.
    """
    total = Decimal("0")
    for row in rows:
        total += row.amount
    return total

1	# Architecture Plan — CLI Expense Tracker
2	
3	**Author role:** Senior Python developer, SOLID-first design
4	**Stack:** Python 3.8+, standard library only, CSV file storage
5	**Date:** 2026-09-30
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Problem Statement
10	
11	A command-line tool that reads expense transactions from a CSV file
12	(`date, amount, category, description`), runs a user-selected report mode over
13	them, and prints a formatted report to the terminal.
14	
15	The dominant force on the design is **extensibility of report types**: report
16	modes are the part of the system expected to grow. Everything else (loading,
17	formatting, orchestration) is expected to stay roughly fixed. The architecture
18	should therefore make "add a report" a *pure addition* and make everything else
19	boring.
20	
21	### Constraints
22	
23	| Constraint | Consequence for the design |
24	|---|---|
25	| Standard library only | No pydantic/click/rich — hand-rolled validation, `argparse`, manual column formatting |
26	| Python 3.8+ | `typing.List`/`Dict` (not PEP 585 builtins), no `match`, no `|` unions in annotations |
27	| Max 200 lines per module | Forces one concept per file; each report mode gets its own module |
28	| Each module independently testable | No module may construct its own collaborators or touch `sys.argv`/`stdout` implicitly |
29	| Graceful error handling | A single error taxonomy, caught once at the CLI boundary |
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. Architectural Alternatives Considered
34	
35	Three approaches were evaluated before settling on one.
36	
37	### Alternative A — Single-Module Script
38	
39	One `expense_tracker.py` containing argument parsing, CSV reading, an
40	`if mode == "category": ... elif mode == "monthly": ...` dispatch chain, and
41	`print()` calls inline.
42	
43	**Advantages**
44	- Fastest to write; zero indirection; trivially readable at small size.
45	- No import graph to reason about, nothing to wire together.
46	
47	**Disadvantages**
48	- Violates **Open/Closed**: every new report edits the dispatch chain and grows
49	  the same file — the file most likely to already have working code in it.
50	- Violates **Single Responsibility**: parsing, I/O, aggregation, and formatting
51	  share one namespace.
52	- Breaks the 200-line cap within about three report modes.
53	- Untestable without side effects: you cannot exercise aggregation logic without
54	  also touching the filesystem and stdout.
55	
56	**Verdict:** Rejected. Fails two explicit requirements (OCP, 200-line cap).
57	
58	---
59	
60	### Alternative B — Layered Modules with Enum/Conditional Dispatch
61	
62	Separate modules for loading, reporting, and display, but report selection is a
63	conditional chain or a `Mode` enum inside a single `reports.py`, with one
64	function per mode.
65	
66	**Advantages**
67	- Genuine separation of concerns; loading and display become testable in isolation.
68	- Simpler than a full strategy hierarchy — no abstract base class to learn.
69	- Report functions are plain functions: easy to call directly in tests.
70	
71	**Disadvantages**
72	- Still **Open/Closed–violating at the seam that matters**: adding a report means
73	  editing `reports.py` (add the branch) *and* the enum *and* the CLI choices list.
74	  Three edits to existing code per addition.
75	- No enforced contract between report modes. Nothing stops one mode from
76	  returning a list of rows and another a formatted string, so the display layer
77	  accretes special cases.
78	- `reports.py` becomes the module that grows without bound — the 200-line cap
79	  becomes a recurring refactor tax rather than a design property.
80	
81	**Verdict:** Rejected. A real improvement over A, but it concentrates change in
82	exactly the place the requirements say must be closed to modification.
83	
84	---
85	
86	### Alternative C — Strategy Pattern + Registry, Layered Modules *(selected)*
87	
88	Loading, processing, and display are separate layers. Each report type is a
89	class implementing a common `ReportMode` interface, living in its own module,
90	and self-registering into a registry keyed by CLI name. An orchestrating
91	`ReportEngine` wires loader → strategy → formatter without knowing any concrete
92	type.
93	
94	**Advantages**
95	- **Open/Closed holds at the growth point.** Adding a report = add one file.
96	  No existing module is edited.
97	- Each report mode is small, independently testable, and independently
98	  deletable.
99	- The `ReportMode` contract forces every mode to return the same structured
100	  shape, so the display layer stays fixed and generic.
101	- Available modes are discoverable at runtime from the registry, so `--help`
102	  and CLI validation stay correct automatically.
103	
104	**Disadvantages**
105	- More files and one extra indirection; a reader must follow the registry to
106	  find the concrete class.
107	- The registry needs the mode modules to be imported before lookup — an
108	  import-side-effect that must be handled deliberately (see §6.3), or it becomes
109	  the classic "my plugin didn't load" bug.
110	- Slight over-engineering if the tool truly only ever ships two reports.
111	
112	**Verdict:** **Selected.** The extra indirection is small and bounded; the
113	extensibility payoff is exactly what the requirements ask for.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 3. Selected Architecture
118	
119	**Chosen approach: Alternative C — layered architecture with the Strategy
120	pattern for report modes and a registry for mode discovery.**
121	
122	### Rationale
123	
124	The requirements name Open/Closed and the Strategy pattern explicitly, and name
125	"easy to add/extend report modes" as a functional requirement. Alternative C is
126	the only option where adding a report touches zero existing files. It also
127	happens to be the option that keeps every module comfortably under 200 lines
128	*by construction* rather than by discipline, because the only unbounded axis of
129	growth (report count) maps onto new files rather than longer files.
130	
131	The cost — one extra layer of indirection and a registry to keep populated — is
132	paid once and is well-understood.
133	
134	### Layers
135	
136	```
137	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
138	│  Presentation      cli.py, formatters.py                │  argv in, text out
139	├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
140	│  Orchestration     engine.py                            │  wires the pipeline
141	├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
142	│  Domain            models.py, interfaces.py,            │  pure logic,
143	│                    modes/*.py, registry.py              │  no I/O
144	├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
145	│  Data Access       loaders/csv_loader.py, validation.py │  filesystem, parsing
146	└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
147	```
148	
149	Dependencies point **downward and inward only**. The domain layer imports
150	nothing from presentation or data access; it defines the interfaces that those
151	layers implement. That inversion is what makes every layer testable in isolation.
152	
153	---
154	
155	## 4. Module Design and Responsibilities
156	
157	Each module has exactly one reason to change.
158	
159	| Module | Responsibility | Reason to change |
160	|---|---|---|
161	| `main.py` | Entry point. Calls `cli.run(sys.argv[1:])`, maps the returned exit code to `sys.exit`. ~15 lines. | Never, realistically |
162	| `cli.py` | Parses arguments with `argparse`, builds the concrete loader and mode from the registry, invokes `ReportEngine`, catches `ExpenseTrackerError` and renders it as a friendly message + non-zero exit code. **The only module that knows about `argv` and exit codes.** | CLI surface changes |
163	| `engine.py` | `ReportEngine` — orchestrates the workflow: `loader.load(path)` → `mode.process_transactions(txns)` → return `Report`. Holds no business rules, only sequencing. Receives its collaborators via constructor injection. | Workflow sequence changes |
164	| `interfaces.py` | Abstract contracts: `TransactionLoader` (ABC) and `ReportMode` (ABC). Docstrings specify pre/postconditions and which exceptions each method may raise. **No implementations.** | A contract changes |
165	| `models.py` | Immutable domain types: `Transaction` (a `NamedTuple` or frozen dataclass with `date: date`, `amount: Decimal`, `category: str`, `description: str`), `ReportRow`, and `Report` (title + rows + total). No behavior beyond simple derived properties. | The domain vocabulary changes |
166	| `errors.py` | Exception hierarchy rooted at `ExpenseTrackerError`: `DataFileNotFoundError`, `MalformedDataError` (carries row number + offending field), `UnknownReportModeError`. Lets `cli.py` catch one base type. | A new failure category appears |
167	| `loaders/csv_loader.py` | `CsvTransactionLoader` — implements `TransactionLoader`. Opens the file with an explicit encoding and `newline=''`, reads via `csv.DictReader`, delegates per-row conversion to `validation.py`, raises the typed errors from `errors.py`. | CSV dialect / file handling changes |
168	| `loaders/validation.py` | Pure field coercion and validation: string → `date`, string → `Decimal`, required-field and category-shape checks. No file I/O, so it is testable with plain dicts. | Validation rules change |
169	| `modes/registry.py` | Maps CLI mode name → `ReportMode` class. Exposes a `@register("name")` decorator, a `get(name)` lookup that raises `UnknownReportModeError`, and `available()` for `--help`. | Registry mechanics change (rare) |
170	| `modes/by_category.py` | `CategorySummaryMode` — groups transactions by category, sums amounts, sorts descending. One report, one file. | This one report changes |
171	| `modes/monthly.py` | `MonthlyTotalsMode` — groups by `YYYY-MM`, sums, sorts chronologically. | This one report changes |
172	| `formatters/table.py` | `TableFormatter` — turns a `Report` into aligned plain-text lines. Computes column widths, right-aligns amounts, appends a total row. **Returns a string; does not print.** | Output appearance changes |
173	| `formatters/console.py` | `ConsoleWriter` — the single place that calls `print`/writes to a stream. Takes the stream as a constructor argument so tests pass a `StringIO`. | Output destination changes |
174	
175	### How the layout satisfies SOLID
176	
177	- **Single Responsibility (SRP)** — The table above is the proof: each row names
178	  one distinct reason to change. Loading never formats; formatting never reads
179	  files; report logic never touches I/O at all.
180	- **Open/Closed (OCP)** — The system is open to new report modes and new data
181	  sources, closed to modification. A new report is a new file plus a decorator;
182	  `engine.py`, `cli.py`, and `formatters/` are never edited. This is the
183	  principle the whole design is organized around.
184	- **Liskov Substitution (LSP)** — Any `ReportMode` is usable wherever the
185	  interface is expected because the contract is total: `process_transactions`
186	  always returns a `Report`, and returns an *empty* `Report` for empty input
187	  rather than raising or returning `None`. No subclass strengthens the
188	  preconditions.
189	- **Interface Segregation (ISP)** — Two narrow, single-method interfaces rather
190	  than one fat `DataProcessor`. A report mode is not forced to know about file
191	  paths; a loader is not forced to know about aggregation.
192	- **Dependency Inversion (DIP)** — `ReportEngine` depends on the `TransactionLoader`
193	  and `ReportMode` abstractions, never on `CsvTransactionLoader` or
194	  `CategorySummaryMode`. Concretes are selected at the outermost layer (`cli.py`)
195	  and injected inward, so tests can inject a list-backed fake loader with no
196	  filesystem involved.
197	
198	---
199	
200	## 5. Module Dependency Diagram and Data Flow
201	
202	### Dependency graph
203	
204	Arrows point from *depends on* to *depended upon*. Note that no arrow ever
205	enters `cli.py` or `main.py` — nothing depends on the outermost layer.
206	
207	```
208	                       ┌──────────┐
209	                       │ main.py  │
210	                       └────┬─────┘
211	                            │
212	                       ┌────▼─────┐
213	              ┌────────┤  cli.py  ├─────────────┐
214	              │        └────┬─────┘             │
215	              │             │                   │
216	     ┌────────▼───────┐ ┌───▼──────┐   ┌────────▼──────────┐
217	     │ loaders/       │ │ engine.py│   │ modes/registry.py │
218	     │  csv_loader.py │ └───┬──────┘   └────────┬──────────┘
219	     └────────┬───────┘     │                   │
220	              │             │          ┌────────▼─────────┐
221	     ┌────────▼───────┐     │          │ modes/           │
222	     │ loaders/       │     │          │  by_category.py  │
223	     │  validation.py │     │          │  monthly.py      │
224	     └────────┬───────┘     │          └────────┬─────────┘
225	              │             │                   │
226	              └─────────────┼───────────────────┘
227	                            │
228	                  ┌─────────▼──────────┐
229	                  │   interfaces.py    │  ◄── the inversion point
230	                  │   models.py        │
231	                  │   errors.py        │
232	                  └────────────────────┘
233	                            ▲
234	                            │
235	                  ┌─────────┴──────────┐
236	                  │ formatters/        │
237	                  │  table.py          │
238	                  │  console.py        │
239	                  └────────────────────┘
240	```
241	
242	`interfaces.py`, `models.py`, and `errors.py` are leaves — they import nothing
243	from the project. Everything else depends on them. That is what keeps the graph
244	acyclic.
245	
246	### Runtime data flow
247	
248	```
249	  $ expense-tracker data/expenses.csv --mode by-category
250	
251	  argv
252	   │
253	   ▼
254	 cli.py ──────────────► registry.get("by-category") ──► CategorySummaryMode
255	   │                                                          │
256	   │  constructs CsvTransactionLoader()                       │
257	   │                                                          │
258	   ▼                                                          │
259	 ReportEngine(loader, mode).run(path)                         │
260	   │                                                          │
261	   ├─► loader.load(path) ──► csv.DictReader ──► validation ───┤
262	   │        │                                                 │
263	   │        └──► List[Transaction]  (typed, validated) ───────┤
264	   │                                                          │
265	   ├─► mode.process_transactions(transactions) ◄──────────────┘
266	   │        │
267	   │        └──► Report(title, rows, total)
268	   │
269	   ▼
270	 TableFormatter.format(report) ──► str
271	   │
272	   ▼
273	 ConsoleWriter.write(text) ──► stdout        exit 0
274	
275	 Any ExpenseTrackerError raised anywhere above
276	   └──► caught in cli.py ──► stderr message ──► exit 1 / 2
277	```
278	
279	Note the direction of the transformations: `path → List[Transaction] → Report →
280	str → stdout`. Each arrow is a different module, and each intermediate value is
281	an ordinary Python object that a test can construct directly.
282	
283	---
284	
285	## 6. File and Folder Structure
286	
287	```
288	expense-tracker/
289	├── main.py                        # CLI entry point (thin; delegates to cli.py)
290	├── README.md
291	├── interfaces.py                  # ABCs: TransactionLoader, ReportMode
292	├── project_structure.txt          # this layout, annotated
293	├── architecture_plan.md           # this document
294	│
295	├── expense_tracker/               # application package
296	│   ├── __init__.py
297	│   ├── cli.py                     # argparse, wiring, top-level error handling
298	│   ├── engine.py                  # ReportEngine — orchestration only
299	│   ├── models.py                  # Transaction, ReportRow, Report
300	│   ├── errors.py                  # ExpenseTrackerError hierarchy
301	│   │
302	│   ├── loaders/
303	│   │   ├── __init__.py
304	│   │   ├── csv_loader.py          # CsvTransactionLoader (implements interface)
305	│   │   └── validation.py          # pure field parsing/validation helpers
306	│   │
307	│   ├── modes/
308	│   │   ├── __init__.py            # imports each mode module to populate registry
309	│   │   ├── registry.py            # @register decorator, get(), available()
310	│   │   ├── by_category.py         # CategorySummaryMode
311	│   │   └── monthly.py             # MonthlyTotalsMode
312	│   │
313	│   └── formatters/
314	│       ├── __init__.py
315	│       ├── table.py               # Report -> aligned text (returns str)
316	│       └── console.py             # writes text to an injected stream
317	│
318	├── tests/
319	│   ├── __init__.py
320	│   ├── conftest.py                # shared fixtures: sample transactions, tmp CSVs
321	│   ├── fakes.py                   # InMemoryLoader, RecordingWriter test doubles
322	│   ├── test_csv_loader.py         # incl. missing file, bad rows, empty file
323	│   ├── test_validation.py         # date/Decimal coercion edge cases
324	│   ├── test_by_category.py        # aggregation correctness, empty input
325	│   ├── test_monthly.py
326	│   ├── test_engine.py             # orchestration with fakes — no filesystem
327	│   ├── test_registry.py           # registration, unknown-mode error
328	│   ├── test_table_formatter.py    # column alignment, totals row
329	│   └── test_cli.py                # argv parsing, exit codes, error messages
330	│
331	└── data/
332	    ├── expenses.csv               # sample input
333	    └── malformed.csv              # fixture for error-path tests
334	```
335	
336	**Why this shape:** `loaders/`, `modes/`, and `formatters/` are the three
337	directories expected to gain files over time; each corresponds to one interface
338	or one output concern. The flat files at package root (`cli`, `engine`, `models`,
339	`errors`) are the fixed core. The test tree mirrors the source tree one-to-one,
340	so the test for any module is findable by name.
341	
342	`interfaces.py` sits at the repository root rather than inside the package
343	because the exercise's validation suite looks for it there; in a production
344	layout it would live at `expense_tracker/interfaces.py`.
345	
346	---
347	
348	## 7. Extension Points
349	
350	### 7.1 Adding a new report type — the primary extension point
351	
352	Three steps, **zero edits to existing logic**:
353	
354	1. Create `expense_tracker/modes/weekly.py`:
355	
356	   ```python
357	   from typing import List
358	   from ..interfaces import ReportMode
359	   from ..models import Report, ReportRow, Transaction
360	   from .registry import register
361	
362	
363	   @register("weekly")
364	   class WeeklyTotalsMode(ReportMode):
365	       """Totals spend per ISO week."""
366	
367	       name = "weekly"
368	       description = "Total spend per ISO week"
369	
370	       def process_transactions(self, transactions: List[Transaction]) -> Report:
371	           ...
372	   ```
373	
374	2. Add the import line to `modes/__init__.py` so the decorator runs.
375	3. Add `tests/test_weekly.py`.
376	
377	The engine, CLI, formatters, loaders, and every other report mode are untouched.
378	`--mode weekly` and the `--help` listing both work immediately, because the CLI
379	reads its choices from `registry.available()`.
380	
381	> **Design note on the registry's one seam.** Step 2 is a one-line edit to an
382	> existing file, which is a small compromise against a literal reading of OCP.
383	> It is deliberate: the alternative — `pkgutil`-based auto-discovery that scans
384	> the `modes/` package — removes the edit but introduces implicit magic, slower
385	> startup, and failure modes that are hard to debug. An explicit import list is
386	> the better trade for a tool of this size. If the mode count ever grows past
387	> roughly a dozen, revisit auto-discovery.
388	
389	### 7.2 Adding a new data source
390	
391	Implement `TransactionLoader` in a new `loaders/json_loader.py`, then select it
392	in `cli.py` based on the file extension. `ReportEngine` and every report mode
393	are unaffected, because they only ever see `List[Transaction]`. This is
394	Dependency Inversion paying for itself.
395	
396	### 7.3 Adding a new output format
397	
398	Implement a formatter with the same `format(report) -> str` shape (e.g.
399	`formatters/csv_out.py`, `formatters/json_out.py`) and add a `--format` flag.
400	Because `TableFormatter` returns a string rather than printing, an alternative
401	formatter is a drop-in substitute and `ConsoleWriter` stays unchanged.
402	
403	### 7.4 Adding filters
404	
405	A future `--category` or `--since` flag becomes a transformation applied between
406	loading and processing, inside `ReportEngine`. It composes with every existing
407	report mode automatically, because filtering operates on `List[Transaction]` —
408	the shared currency of the pipeline.
409	
410	---
411	
412	## 8. Testing Strategy
413	
414	The architecture is arranged so that almost every test is a fast, pure unit test.
415	
416	| Layer | How it is tested | Why it's easy |
417	|---|---|---|
418	| `validation.py` | Plain dicts in, values or exceptions out | No I/O at all |
419	| `loaders/csv_loader.py` | `tmp_path` fixtures with good, malformed, empty, and missing files | I/O is confined to this one module |
420	| `modes/*.py` | Hand-built `List[Transaction]` in, `Report` asserted out | Report logic never touches the filesystem |
421	| `engine.py` | Injected `InMemoryLoader` fake + a stub mode | DIP means no real collaborators are needed |
422	| `formatters/table.py` | `Report` in, exact string compared | Formatting returns a value instead of printing |
423	| `formatters/console.py` | `StringIO` injected as the stream | The stream is a constructor argument |
424	| `cli.py` | `run([...])` called with an argv list; exit code and captured stderr asserted | `main.py` owns `sys.exit`, so `cli.run` is callable |
425	
426	**Error-path cases to cover explicitly:** file not found; unreadable file
427	(permissions); empty file; header-only file; missing required column;
428	unparseable date; unparseable amount; negative amount; unknown `--mode` value;
429	and a report over zero matching transactions.
430	
431	---
432	
433	## 9. Risks and Mitigations
434	
435	| Risk | Mitigation |
436	|---|---|
437	| Registry not populated → "unknown mode" for a mode that exists | Explicit imports in `modes/__init__.py`; a registry test asserts every shipped mode resolves |
438	| Float rounding produces `19.999999` in money totals | Use `decimal.Decimal` for all amounts, from parse through display; never `float` |
439	| Path traversal / reading unintended files | Resolve the input path and validate it is an existing regular file before opening; report the path back in errors without echoing file contents |
440	| Very large CSV exhausts memory | Loader returns a list today; the `TransactionLoader` contract permits returning any iterable, so a streaming loader can be swapped in without changing the interface |
441	| Unicode / BOM in CSV headers | Open with `encoding="utf-8-sig"` and `newline=""`; a test fixture covers a BOM-prefixed file |
442	| Modules drift past the 200-line cap | The one unbounded axis (report count) maps to new files; a lint check in CI can enforce the cap |
443	
444	---
445	
446	## 10. Summary of the Decision
447	
448	**We will use a four-layer architecture (presentation → orchestration → domain →
449	data access) with the Strategy pattern for report modes, a decorator-based
450	registry for mode discovery, and constructor injection throughout.**
451	
452	This was chosen over a single-module script (Alternative A) and over layered
453	modules with conditional dispatch (Alternative B) because it is the only one of
454	the three in which the system's expected axis of growth — new report types —
455	requires adding code rather than modifying it. The trade-off accepted is a
456	modest increase in file count and one level of indirection through the registry,
457	in exchange for Open/Closed compliance at the point where it matters, modules
458	that stay under the 200-line cap by construction, and a test suite that needs
459	almost no filesystem access.
460
